questions.stem: Why does a convolutional layer use far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer on the same image?
choices: It processes fewer pixels
Weights are shared: one small kernel slides across the whole image instead of every input pixel having its own weight to every output
It uses lower precision
It skips the bias term
questions.explanation: Weight sharing is the core idea. A 3x3 kernel has nine weights per channel pair regardless of image size, whereas a dense layer needs a weight per input-output pair. Sharing also builds in translation equivariance: a pattern is detected wherever it occurs.

questions.stem: What is a neuron's receptive field, and why does it grow with depth?
choices: The number of channels it sees; it grows because channels increase
The region of the input that can influence it; each layer aggregates a neighbourhood of the previous layer, so the reachable input area compounds with depth
The size of the output feature map
The batch dimension
questions.explanation: A 3x3 convolution sees 3x3 of its input, but that input already summarised a neighbourhood, so two stacked 3x3 layers see 5x5 of the original image. Stride and pooling accelerate the growth. If the receptive field never covers the object, the network cannot represent it as a whole.

questions.stem: Two stacked 3x3 convolutions are often preferred to one 5x5. Why?
choices: They are easier to implement
They cover the same receptive field with fewer parameters and add an extra non-linearity between them
5x5 kernels cannot be trained
They use more memory, which improves accuracy
questions.explanation: Two 3x3 layers reach 5x5 of the input using 18 weights per channel pair against 25, and interpose an activation that a single large kernel cannot. That combination of cheaper and more expressive is why VGG standardised on small kernels and why the pattern persists.

questions.stem: What does stride 2 in a convolution accomplish?
choices: It doubles the number of channels
It halves the spatial resolution, downsampling while convolving instead of using a separate pooling layer
It doubles the kernel size
It skips every second channel
questions.explanation: Stride sets the step between kernel applications, so stride 2 produces an output roughly half the height and width. Many modern architectures use strided convolutions rather than pooling because the downsampling is then learned rather than fixed.

questions.stem: What does dilated (atrous) convolution buy you?
choices: Fewer channels
A larger receptive field without more parameters or loss of resolution, by spacing the kernel taps apart
Faster training always
Automatic padding
questions.explanation: Inserting gaps between kernel taps widens the field of view at constant parameter count and without downsampling. That matters for dense prediction such as segmentation, where you need context but cannot afford to throw away spatial resolution.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about batch normalisation are correct?
choices: It normalises activations using statistics computed over the batch during training
At inference it uses running statistics accumulated during training, which is why model.eval() matters
It normalises the input image only
It removes the need for a learning rate
questions.explanation: BatchNorm standardises each channel using the current batch's mean and variance while training, and switches to accumulated running estimates at inference so predictions do not depend on batch composition. Forgetting eval() leaves it using batch statistics, which makes single-image inference unstable.

questions.stem: Why does batch normalisation behave poorly with very small batch sizes, and what is used instead?
choices: It cannot be computed below batch size 8
Batch statistics become noisy estimates, so normalisation is unstable; GroupNorm or LayerNorm, which normalise within an example, are used instead
It requires a GPU
Small batches overflow the running statistics
questions.explanation: With two or four samples the per-batch mean and variance are poor estimates and fluctuate wildly between steps. Group normalisation splits channels into groups and normalises within a single example, removing the batch dependence entirely — which is why detection and segmentation models trained at small batch sizes often use it.

questions.stem: What problem do residual connections solve?
choices: They reduce the parameter count
They give gradients a direct path through the network, making very deep stacks trainable rather than degrading as depth increases
They remove the need for normalisation
They increase the receptive field
questions.explanation: Before ResNet, adding layers past a point made training error worse, not just validation error. Skip connections let a block learn a residual on top of the identity, so gradients flow around it and depth stops being an obstacle. It is what made hundred-layer networks practical.

questions.stem: What is a depthwise separable convolution?
choices: A convolution split across two GPUs
A depthwise convolution applying one filter per input channel, followed by a 1x1 pointwise convolution mixing channels — far cheaper than a full convolution
A convolution with no bias
Two convolutions run in parallel and summed
questions.explanation: Factorising spatial filtering from channel mixing cuts the cost by roughly the kernel area compared with a standard convolution. That efficiency is what makes MobileNet-class architectures viable on phones and embedded devices.

questions.stem: What does a 1x1 convolution actually do?
choices: Nothing useful, since the kernel covers one pixel
Mixes information across channels at each spatial position, which lets it change channel depth cheaply and add non-linearity
Blurs the image
Increases spatial resolution
questions.explanation: A 1x1 kernel has no spatial extent but full channel extent, so it is a per-pixel linear combination across channels. It is the standard way to expand or reduce depth — the bottleneck blocks in ResNet and the pointwise stage of separable convolutions both rely on it.

questions.stem: What does global average pooling replace, and what does that change?
choices: Batch normalisation; it stabilises training
The flatten-plus-dense head; it averages each channel to one value, removing a huge parameter block and making the network tolerant of input size
The activation function; it adds non-linearity
The loss function; it changes the objective
questions.explanation: Flattening a feature map into a dense layer creates most of a classic CNN's parameters and hard-codes the input resolution. Averaging each channel yields a fixed-length vector regardless of spatial size, which both regularises and lets the same network accept different input dimensions.

questions.stem: You fine-tune an ImageNet backbone on 2,000 medical images. Which TWO choices are sound?
choices: Freeze most of the backbone initially and train the head, then unfreeze the later layers with a low learning rate
Use strong augmentation appropriate to the domain, since 2,000 images is far too few to learn features from scratch
Train all layers from random initialisation
Remove batch normalisation layers
questions.explanation: With limited data the pretrained features are the asset. Training the head first avoids destroying them with large early gradients, and gradual unfreezing at a low rate adapts them gently. Augmentation multiplies effective data. Random initialisation discards precisely what makes the transfer work.

questions.stem: Early layers of a pretrained CNN are often reused unchanged even across very different domains. Why?
choices: They contain the most parameters
They learn generic low-level structure — edges, colours, textures — that is common to almost all natural images, while later layers become task-specific
They train fastest
They are the only layers without normalisation
questions.explanation: Visualisations consistently show first-layer filters resembling oriented edges and colour blobs regardless of the training set, with specificity emerging deeper. That is the empirical basis of transfer learning, and why the depth at which you start unfreezing tracks how far your domain sits from the source.

questions.stem: What is the practical difference between max pooling and average pooling?
choices: Max pooling is faster
Max pooling keeps the strongest activation, preserving whether a feature was present; average pooling smooths, preserving overall magnitude
Average pooling has learnable weights
Max pooling doubles resolution
questions.explanation: Max is a detector: it reports the most salient response in the window and discards the rest, which suits presence-of-feature reasoning. Averaging retains aggregate intensity, which is why it appears at the end of networks for pooling whole feature maps rather than in the middle.

questions.stem: Your CNN classifies well but fails when objects appear at the image edge. What is the most likely architectural cause?
choices: Too few channels
Padding and receptive field effects: border regions are seen by fewer kernel applications and padded with zeros, so edge context differs from centre context
The learning rate is too high
Batch normalisation is disabled
questions.explanation: Zero padding fabricates a border that the network learns to treat as a cue, and edge pixels participate in fewer overlapping windows. Training augmentation with translation and random cropping, or reflective padding, reduces the asymmetry. It is a real and under-appreciated source of position bias.

questions.stem: Why can a fully convolutional network accept variable input sizes while a CNN ending in dense layers cannot?
choices: Convolutions have no parameters
A dense layer fixes the flattened feature length, whereas convolution and pooling scale their output with the input
Dense layers require grayscale
Convolutions are faster
questions.explanation: A dense layer's weight matrix is sized to a specific flattened dimension, so any other input size produces a shape mismatch. Convolution and pooling are shape-agnostic, which is what lets fully convolutional networks handle arbitrary resolutions and produce dense spatial outputs for segmentation.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a feature pyramid in a backbone?
choices: To reduce the number of layers
To provide features at several spatial resolutions, so small objects can be detected from high-resolution shallow maps and large ones from deep semantic maps
To compress the model
To replace batch normalisation
questions.explanation: A single deep feature map has strong semantics but coarse resolution, which loses small objects. A pyramid combines resolutions, typically with top-down connections that push semantic information back into finer maps. Multi-scale representation is central to modern detection and segmentation.

questions.stem: Given a fixed compute budget, EfficientNet argues you should scale what?
choices: Depth only
Depth, width and input resolution together in a balanced ratio, rather than any one dimension alone
Batch size only
The number of classes
questions.explanation: Scaling one dimension saturates: deeper networks stop helping, wider ones stop adding information, higher resolution outgrows the receptive field. Compound scaling raises all three by a coefficient tuned once, which reaches better accuracy per FLOP than scaling any single axis.

questions.stem: Why is a CNN translation-equivariant but not naturally rotation-invariant?
choices: Rotations are computationally harder
Weight sharing slides the same kernel across positions, so a shifted input shifts the response; nothing in the architecture ties together rotated versions of a filter
Pooling removes rotation information
Convolutions only work on axis-aligned features
questions.explanation: The convolution structure builds in the shift symmetry and nothing else. Rotational robustness must come from augmentation, from architectures designed with rotational symmetry, or from the data itself already containing rotated examples.

questions.stem: What does the channel dimension represent after several convolutional layers?
choices: Colour channels, always three
Learned feature detectors: each channel is a map of where its particular pattern responds
Batch elements
Spatial coordinates
questions.explanation: Only the input layer's channels are colours. After that each channel is the response map of one learned filter — an edge orientation early on, a texture or part detector deeper. Feature-map visualisation and channel attention both rest on this reading.

questions.stem: A backbone must run at 30 FPS on an embedded GPU. Which TWO architectural choices are appropriate?
choices: Depthwise separable convolutions to cut FLOPs at similar accuracy
A smaller input resolution, since cost scales with the square of the spatial dimensions
Adding more residual blocks for accuracy
Replacing all convolutions with dense layers
questions.explanation: Separable convolutions and resolution are the two biggest levers on inference cost, and resolution is quadratic so it dominates. Adding blocks moves the wrong way, and dense layers would explode both parameters and compute while discarding spatial structure.

questions.stem: Why is ReLU the default activation in most CNNs?
choices: It is the only non-linear function available
It is cheap to compute and does not saturate for positive inputs, so gradients flow rather than vanishing as they do with sigmoid or tanh
It normalises the output
It guarantees convergence
questions.explanation: Sigmoid and tanh flatten at both extremes, so gradients shrink toward zero and deep stacks train badly. ReLU has constant gradient on the positive side and costs a comparison. Its weakness is dead units on the negative side, which variants like LeakyReLU address.
